title: Cap. VIII: Chamier — alien guilt alone does not damn infants
pass_a_gloss: Placeus says he took the next stroke from Chamier. Chamier asks: if infants have no sin of their own, why do they die a death that is their own? Divine justice will not carry a fault that is merely someone else's. Human law may once have made a father's slavery pass to the sons as inheritance; nothing like that stood among God's people under the divine statutes — and still less in God himself, who grows angry at the people who kept saying the proverb about fathers eating sour grapes and children's teeth going dull.
pass_b_english: I took this from Chamier. "If infants," he says, "have nothing of their own sin, why do they perish by their own death? For divine justice does not bear an alien fault that is only alien. Men may once have had the custom that a father's slavery was hereditary for the sons; but nothing of that kind stood in the people of God under the divine laws — how much less in God, who is angry at those who had in their mouth the proverb, Our fathers ate sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge" (Ezekiel 18:2).
source_text: Hoc accepi a Chamiero, Si nihil, inquit, habent infantes peccati proprii, cur propria morte pereunt? Nam propter alienam culpam, quae tantum aliena sit, non fert justitia divina. Habuerint sane aliquando homines eum morem, ut patris servitus, filiis esset hereditaria: at ejusmodi nihil erat in populo Dei, ex divinis legibus: quanto minus in Deo: qui irascitur in eos, quibus erat in ore proverbium, Patres nostri uvas acerbas comederunt: Filiis autem dentes stupent;

choices.decision: Divine justice does not bear/allow purely alien fault as damning ground
Inline Ezekiel 18:2; same proverb also Jer 31:29 — Placeus wording tracks Ez
